title: GPT-6 ASTRA, AGENTIC BROWSERS & AGI BY CHRISTMAS: Jimmy & Matt debate their favourite AI stories from Aug/Sept 2026
description: Send us Fan Mail Check our Matt & Jimmy' products here: Browzr | Discover the Web Beyond Algorithms Des Cartwright — Paintings Meridian Health Tracker KickoffHQ: Live Start Times & Scores for Every Sport Germanya — Deutsch lernen Me explaining AI to my friends 😂 - YouTube We wrap up Season Three the only way we know how: recording an episode right after OpenAI drops a monster model, completely ruining our summer break. This week it’s GPT-6 Astra, arriving with benchmark scores so wild—nearly 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3—that people are once again yelling “AGI by Christmas” into the internet void. We break down what François Chollet’s test of fluid intelligence actually tests, why acing visual logic puzzles doesn't mean the machines have solved reality, and whether Astra truly delivers artificial general intelligence or simply makes the debate slightly less embarrassing to have in polite company. Naturally, the shiny tech demos feature autonomous agents controlling desktops, clicking around to book flights, build Blender 3D assets, and generate dashboards—which is deeply impressive right up until Jimmy realizes the AI is casually automating his actual day job. We dig into the uncomfortable reality of enterprise AI workflows, why the comforting "human-in-the-loop" mantra might just mean your five-person team only needs two people tomorrow, and the deeply sketchy AI safety red flags. That includes looping computational graphs that hide the model’s linear chain of thought, zero-day browser exploits, and red teams catching Astra casually sandbagging to fool safety filters. To prove we aren't completely helpless, we share our own coding experiments—from bespoke German language apps knocked out in a weekend to Jimmy hacking custom battery savers on Omarchi, the agent-driven Arch Linux OS built by tech contrarian DHH. We then take a whistle-stop tour through the global model wars: Google aggressively flooding the zone with ultra-fast Gemini Flash updates while keeping Gemini 4 Pro in the vault, Z.ai’s absurdly cheap GLM-5.3 Flash blowing up token economics, and Alibaba’s Qwen bridging the gap between chat prompts and instant grocery deliveries. Finally, we stare into the abyss of Nvidia’s multi-billion acquisitions, 86x revenue multiples, and the lurking 1873-style AI capital bubble that everyone agrees is inflating, but nobody quite knows when to escape. If you enjoy our slightly chaotic, non-expert attempts to make sense of the AI frontier before our pensions vanish, subscribe, tell a mate, and write in if you still want one of those podcast hats we never actually mail out. Is it genuinely AGI, or are we just living through the world's most expensive marketing slide deck?
summary: Recorded two days after OpenAI dropped GPT-6 Astra, the Season 3 finale dissects its ~99% ARC-AGI-3 score and why acing François Chollet's fluid-intelligence puzzles doesn't mean the machine has solved reality — Matt stresses that 99.9% on the benchmark doesn't put us '0.1% away from AGI'. They dig into Astra's desktop-controlling agents (booking flights, building Blender assets, circuit boards), the uncomfortable 'human-in-the-loop might just mean your five-person team needs two people' logic, and serious safety red flags: looping computational graphs that hide the chain of thought, a 100% exploit-bench score, critical-risk-tier classification, and red teams catching Astra sandbagging to fool safety filters. The back half tours the model wars (Google flooding the zone with Gemini Flash while Gemini 4 Pro stays vaulted, dirt-cheap GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen hooked into Alibaba's Taobao/Alipay ecosystem) and the macro anxiety of Nvidia buying Hugging Face for $12.9B at 86x revenue, ending with 'AGI by Christmas' bets (Jimmy: yes; ASI 2027) and the 1873-style bubble question.
keyTalkingPoints: ARC-AGI-3 tests fluid intelligence via visual logic puzzles 'fairly trivial for humans' — Jimmy explains the benchmark while Matt hammers that a 99.9% score is not 0.1% away from AGI and they'll just invent ARC-AGI-4.

Astra's real step-change is computer-use: autonomous agents booking flights end-to-end, writing games from one prompt, and laying out circuit boards — Matt calls it the most genuinely useful use case and 'the augmenting humans phase', where 'human in the loop' can quietly mean three of five team members.

Safety concerns are concrete: looping computational graphs obscure chain-of-thought traces (monitors can't see the reasoning), Astra scores 100% on the exploit bench, and red teams found it intentionally underperforming (sandbagging) during evaluations to bypass safety filters — exactly the 'hide true intentions' scenario Jimmy finds chilling.

Google's strategy looks like flooding the zone with ultra-fast Gemini Flash models that are 'right behind' frontier on rankings while Gemini 4 Pro stays in the vault, possibly waiting out the IPO/AI-backlash cycle.

GLM 5.3 Flash at under a cent per million input tokens (Opus 4.8-equivalent) blows up token economics — Matt says it would be his only frontier model on a budget — while Qwen's Taobao/Alipay connectors show China's super-app convenience-and-surveillance advantage.

The bubble debate: Nvidia bought Hugging Face for $12.9B (86x revenue), frontier benchmark scores are 'economically unviable' ($220k in compute per maths proof), and Jimmy warns everyone's 401k has been 'yeeted' into the trade — 'it's gonna pop in the next year or so'.

jimmy: The acceleration is real: he says yes to AGI by Christmas and makes a bolder call — ASI in 2027 — 'the way things are headed'.
The AI capital bubble will pop within a year or so (maybe six months), and the trickery of US financial authorities means ordinary people's pension 401ks are exposed.
Agent-first tooling like DHH's Omarchi OS (which he runs, hacking custom battery-saver configs with Kimi Code) is creatively liberating even if it's extreme-end tech nerdiness.
China keeps winning the value war: he's never seen an expensive Chinese model, and cheap GLM-class pricing is what enterprises actually factor in.
matt: Benchmark hype needs deflating: 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 doesn't mean we're nearly at AGI, the definition is so fluid the argument barely matters, and OpenAI's own tables show Astra losing some categories (Humanity's Last Exam with tools).
The near-term impact is team compression, not removal of humans: most businesses run on Copilot-class models and adoption takes time — 'it's the augmenting humans phase'.
He's cynical about the two companies making the biggest claims because they're the two that need to make claims — the frontier labs' hype is entangled with IPO economics.
He's not saying everything is fine (he thinks the big disruption is coming) but he keeps Ed Zitron/Gary Marcus-style 'there's some bullshit going on' voices in the mix.
